# Teaching notes: from bacterial classes to trait logic

::: {.callout-warning}
## For teaching staff · draft for discussion
This page is not part of the student text. It maps the current MD1140 microbiology sessions onto the
approach used in this draft, as a starting point for discussion.
:::

## The proposal in brief {#sec-tn-brief}

The proposal keeps the sessions organised by bacterial class and changes what holds each session
together. At present a class session tends to run from organism to infections, then to diagnosis and
then to antibiotics, repeated for each organism. Students meet many organism–disease–drug combinations
with no shared structure, so they try to memorise them.

The alternative keeps the same classes and asks the same six questions of each:

1. What is it built from?
2. How does it get energy, and what does it need to grow?
3. How does it copy itself and change?
4. Where does it live, and how does it spread?
5. How does damage happen, and how much of it comes from the microbe and how much from the host?
6. What does it have that my cells lack?

Each class session then explains why the class behaves as it does. The specific infections,
diagnostic pathways and drug choices move to the organ-system blocks and pharmacology, where students
attach them to a structure they already have.

No trial has compared the two approaches in medical students, so the case rests on expert consensus
and on learning research from other fields:

- The 2026 AMSMIC core objectives make the foundational layer pathogen-free and call for medical
  microbiology to move beyond the "bug parade" [@bauler2026objectives].
- Students taught the causal mechanisms behind clinical features kept more a week later than students
  taught feature lists: 62% against 51% correct, in neurological and rheumatological conditions
  [@woods2006basic].
- Actively comparing two similar cases teaches more than studying each alone [@alfieri2013contrasting].
- Retrieval practice with feedback, spaced over weeks, is among the best-supported study methods.

The full evidence review is in the project's research report.

## Session crosswalk {#sec-tn-crosswalk}

For each session, the table shows what stays as foundation content, what can move later, and where
this draft already covers it. Names in italics are chapters of this book; "outline" marks a chapter
that is planned but not yet written.

::: {.column-page}

| Session | Keep at foundation level | Move to organ-system blocks | Move to pharmacology | In this draft |
|------------------|------------------------------------|------------------|------------|----------------|
| Introduction to microbiology and infectious diseases | Scale; prokaryote versus eukaryote; most microbes are harmless; the six questions | None | None | *The microbial world*; *How bacteria are built and get energy* |
| How microbes cause disease | Colonisation versus disease; damage from microbe versus host; toxins, invasion, survival in cells; host factors | Named diseases | None | *Microbes and their hosts* |
| Staphylococci and streptococci | Gram-positive cocci; clusters versus chains; catalase; why infections are pyogenic; carriage | Skin, throat, heart and bone infections | Drug choice; MRSA | *Gram-positive cocci* (the full test chapter) |
| Infections caused by Enterobacterales | Gram-negative facultative gut rods; LPS; harmless residents versus strains with extra genes | Gut, urinary and bloodstream infections | Resistant strains in detail | *Enterobacterales* (outline); map and contrast pair in *A map of the bacteria* |
| Case studies (F2F) | Recast as mechanism or investigation cases instead of diagnose-and-treat cases | Clinical cases | None | One case per chapter, for example the lab case in *How bacteria are built and get energy* and the outbreak case in *Gram-positive cocci* |
| Epidemiology of infectious diseases | Reservoirs, routes, incubation, carriers, outbreaks, One Health | Syndrome-specific epidemiology | None | *Transmission, outbreaks and One Health* |
| Diagnostic bacteriology | What each method reads: stains read the envelope, culture reads growth needs, molecular tests read sequence, serology reads the host | Which test for which syndrome | None | *Detecting and controlling microbes*; Gram stain and oxygen tube in *How bacteria are built and get energy* |
| Fastidious Gram-negative infections | "Fastidious" as lost biosynthesis; why enriched media work | Respiratory and heart-valve infections | Drug choice | *Fastidious Gram-negatives and Gram-negative cocci* (outline) |
| Pseudomonads, vibrios and Burkholderia | Environmental Gram-negatives; metabolism predicts habitat; intrinsic resistance; melioidosis and diabetes as a host-factor example | Healthcare-associated infections; cholera; melioidosis presentations | Anti-pseudomonal drugs | *Environmental Gram-negatives* (outline); contrast pair in *A map of the bacteria*; melioidosis case in *Microbes and their hosts* |
| Infections caused by Gram-negative cocci | Fragility explains close-contact spread; the capsule in the blood | Meningitis; gonorrhoea | Treatment and prophylaxis | *Fastidious Gram-negatives and Gram-negative cocci* (outline) |
| Anaerobic infections | Why oxygen harms anaerobes; oxygen-poor niches; abscess formation; sample handling | Abdominal, dental and other mixed infections | Drug choice | Oxygen sections and lab case in *How bacteria are built and get energy*; *Anaerobes* (outline) |
| Infections caused by Gram-positive bacilli | Spores; disease from a single toxin; *Listeria* growing in the cold and inside cells | Tetanus, botulism, diphtheria presentations | Drug choice | *Gram-positive rods* (outline) |
| Infections caused by spiral bacteria | Internal flagella and corkscrew motility; hard to see or grow, so detected indirectly; ticks and rats as reservoirs | Syphilis stages; leptospirosis; Lyme disease | Drug choice | *Spiral bacteria* (outline) |
| Atypical infections: *Chlamydia*, *Mycoplasma*, *Rickettsia* | Two reasons the toolkit fails: no wall, or growth only inside cells; what each predicts for staining, culture and drug targets | Atypical pneumonia; sexually transmitted chlamydia; rickettsial fevers | Drug choice | Worked example in *A map of the bacteria*; *Atypicals and mycobacteria* (outline) |
| Infection control practical and STD case management (F2F) | Sterilisation versus disinfection; why alcohol rub misses spores; transmission routes | Case management | None | *Detecting and controlling microbes*; *Transmission, outbreaks and One Health* |
| Antibiotic resistance: threats and stewardship | Selection acts on existing variation; gene transfer; the belief that "the body becomes resistant" corrected; stewardship as a population measure | Resistance in specific infections | Drug classes and mechanisms | *How bacteria copy themselves and change*; MRSA in *Gram-positive cocci* |

:::

## Before and after: the atypicals session {#sec-tn-before-after}

The same 60-minute self-directed session, in two forms. The first column is a typical class-based
outline, not a transcript of any particular session.

| | Class-based outline | Trait-based outline |
|---|---|---|
| Organising idea | Three organisms, each in turn | Two reasons the usual toolkit fails |
| Opening | Definitions and classification | Predict: "A bacterium has no wall. What will the Gram stain, culture and wall-targeting drugs show?" |
| Main part | For each organism: features, diseases, clinical picture, diagnosis, treatment | *Mycoplasma* profile, predicted slot by slot (about 15 minutes); *Mycoplasma* versus *Chlamydia* contrast and sort (10 minutes); *Rickettsia* as a second organism that grows only inside cells, adding vectors (5 minutes) |
| Practice | End-of-session MCQs on facts | Mixed retrieval on the bacteria map: name the group from its traits (10 minutes) |
| Disease detail | Full, for each organism | A short list of where students will meet each organism again in the respiratory and genitourinary blocks |
| What students take away | About 15 organism–disease–drug facts | Two ideas that predict those facts when students meet them later |

The trait-based version is built in this draft, in the section *Worked example: why "atypical"?* of
*A map of the bacteria*.

## Depth and coverage: the group-chapter budget {#sec-tn-depth}

*Gram-positive cocci* is the test case for how deep a group chapter should go. It covers the content
of the "Staphylococci and streptococci" session within this budget:

| Element | Budget in the test chapter |
|---|---|
| Main organisms | Three (*S. aureus*, *S. pyogenes*, *S. pneumoniae*), each with a full profile card |
| Supporting organisms | Four, one table row each: where it lives, the separating trait, why it matters |
| Diseases | Only as patterns of harm: a mechanism, then one named example. No clinical features or diagnostic criteria |
| Laboratory tests | Only those that read a trait: catalase, coagulase, haemolysis, Lancefield group |
| Drugs | None by name. Resistance appears once, as a concept (MRSA as an altered drug target) |
| Activities | Sorting key, three profiles, two contrast pairs, a quiz with mixed items, flashcards, one outbreak case |
| Length | About 2,500 to 3,000 words, roughly one self-directed session |

Three questions for the meeting follow from the budget. Are three main organisms enough? Are any of the
supporting organisms important enough to be main organisms? And is one named example per mechanism
enough for MD1140, or does the course need more disease names at this stage?

## What a session looks like in this format {#sec-tn-template}

Each class session in this draft uses the same parts, which makes sessions quicker to write and easier
for students to navigate:

- [ ] Open with one prediction that students can answer by reasoning from earlier material.
- [ ] Answer the six questions at foundation level only.
- [ ] Include one or two contrast pairs, chosen from the confusions students actually make.
- [ ] Give each example organism a profile card, with some slots left for students to predict.
- [ ] Add a refutation box wherever a common misconception exists.
- [ ] End with a short "later in the course" note naming what the organ-system blocks will add.
- [ ] Write quiz items that ask why, with feedback that explains the mechanism.
- [ ] Add a few flashcards for spaced review.

## Questions for discussion {#sec-tn-questions}

| Topic | Question |
|---|---|
| Scope | Which disease, diagnosis and drug facts must stay in MD1140, and which can move to the organ-system blocks or pharmacology? |
| Contrast pairs | Which organisms do students most often confuse? Those pairs should drive the comparison activities |
| Session titles | Should "Infections caused by Enterobacterales" become something like "How Enterobacterales live", to signal the change in emphasis? |
| Assessment | If teaching shifts to mechanisms, should MCQs shift to questions that ask why? |
| Other organisms | Viruses, fungi and parasites are only outlined here. Would you like to co-design those chapters? |
| Evaluation | Could one session be piloted next year, with a short concept check before and after? No data exist on Singapore medical students' misconceptions about microbiology, so the results would also be publishable |
